29136-harper-s-young-people-september-14:
The September 14, 1880 number of Harper's Young People, volume one, number forty-six, sold for four cents from Harper and Brothers in New York. Its leading story, Who Was Paul Grayson, by John Habberton, author of Helen's Babies, opens at Mr. Morton's select school in Laketon village. The boys are certain no teacher ever rings the bell except at the very instant when yard fun is highest and they least want to come in.

On one bright May morning, all the boys except Bert Sharp are already inside. Bert, with three absences unexplained and no note from his father, cudgels his wits by the open door. A front picture, drawn by T. Thulstrup, shows calling the roll. Readers get a school story with a mystery at its heart: a new pupil, and the question of who he really is.
29148-harper-s-young-people-september-21:
Harper and Brothers published this issue of Harper's Young People, an illustrated weekly for children, on September 21, 1880. Priced at four cents, the issue mixes stories, history, and nature notes, all aimed at young readers. Its lead story, by Emily Leland, follows two farm children, eight-year-old Kitty and seven-year-old Ted, who spend a night away from home after a visit to relatives.

Other pieces include Charles Carleton Coffin's notes on old times in the colonies. There is an account of Lovewell's fight with the Pigwackets. There is also a serial chapter of John Habberton's Who Was Paul Grayson. Short items explain how a crab sheds its shell and how steel pens are made. Readers get a lively snapshot of what American children read for pleasure in 1880.
29154-harper-s-young-people-september-28:
Harper and Brothers published this issue of Harper's Young People, an illustrated weekly for children, on September 28, 1880. Its opening piece describes a children's paradise in Paris. The Jardin d'Acclimatation is a garden in the Bois de Boulogne where young visitors could see tame animals and play without fear of savage beasts.

Other pieces include George Varney's story of Frank's war with raccoons. There is a further chapter of John Habberton's serial Who Was Paul Grayson. Notes cover Japanese life, fording a river in Central Asia, and a short history of the potato. Readers get a varied weekly bundle of travel, nature, and adventure writing, pitched at children and illustrated throughout.
40657-the-quest-the-authorized-translati:
Frederik van Eeden wrote The Quest, known in Dutch as De Kleine Johannes. Laura Ward Cole made the authorized English translation. Mitchell Kennerley published it in New York and London in 1911. The tale follows a boy called Little Johannes.

The narrator warns that the story reads like a fairy tale. All the same, he insists that everything in it really happened. Johannes lives in an old house with a big garden. The house holds dark halls, stairs, and garrets to explore. He names each discovery as he finds it. The caterpillar loft and the chicken room stand indoors. Raspberry Mountain, Gooseberry Woods, and Strawberry Valley stand outdoors. Behind all lies a pond-side spot he calls Paradise, where water-lilies float and reeds whisper with the wind.
49178-harper-s-young-people-september-13:
Harper's Young People for September 13, 1881 is Volume Two Number Ninety Eight of a weekly for youth, sold at four cents. Harper and Brothers issued it at New York at one dollar fifty a year in advance. A front print shows the arrival of the first steamboat. The lead tale is A Two-Headed Family by George Cary Eggleston.

Eggleston calls it a true tale of what two boys did. Bob Towne ran away and took his small brother Ned with him. All in their small Mississippi town talked of the flight. Folk called Bob odd for his love of books and his lone ways. His mother held a letter from Bob that showed he was not hard of heart. She read it again and again and said no word of it.
49213-harper-s-young-people-september-20:
Harper's Young People for September 20, 1881 is an issue of an illustrated weekly for children. Harper and Brothers published it in New York at four cents a copy. The issue opens with a poem, Right About Face, by Mary Brine. In it September orders the children to turn their backs on summer.

The poem marches girls and boys away from woods, ponds, and hills toward lessons and books. A frontispiece shows the last day at the sea-side. The weekly mixed verse, stories, and pictures for young readers. This number catches the end of vacation in 1881, when school called children back from the shore.
49303-harper-s-young-people-september-27:
Harper's Young People for the twenty-seventh of September 1881 is one weekly number of Harper's illustrated magazine for children, volume two, number 100, priced at four cents. Its chief feature in this instalment is chapter nine of Tim and Tip, a serial by James Otis about a boy and his dog, begun in the August numbers.

The chapter is the famous bear-hunt. Tim, a homeless boy taken in by the Tucker family, is allowed two weeks of freedom before school. Bill Thompson arms with a carving knife and a shotgun whose lock he carries in his pocket. He proves the knife by shaving half a shingle in five minutes. Bobby contributes an army musket loaded with firecracker powder and small stones. The comedy of over-armed boys is the chapter's whole delight.
59600-harper-s-young-people-september-12:
Harper Young People for September 12, 1882, is a weekly issue for the young. Harper and Brothers sold it at New York for four cents a copy. Volume three, number one hundred fifty, it carries tales and fact pieces. The Cruise of the Canoe Club, by Alden, runs as its serial lead.

Chapter five strands the boy canoeists in a rapid on their trip. Harry canoe grounds on a rock, and the rest jam close behind. The boys wade, drag their craft by the stern, and scrape their knees. A soft sawdust bank from the Magog mill makes their camp that night. Spacing the canoes wider is the lesson Harry draws for tomorrow.
59628-harper-s-young-people-september-19:
Harper's Young People, an illustrated weekly for children, cost four cents for its issue of Tuesday, September 19, 1882, or $1.50 a year in advance. Its lead story, by Elizabeth Abercrombie, tells of a great mammoth found in Siberian ice. The hero is Ossip Schumachoff, an ivory hunter on the river Lena.

In 1799 Ossip found a block of ice holding an enormous tusked animal, perfectly preserved. Superstition held him off for years, while old men and women of his tribe warned of death to any who saw such a monster. At last he sawed off the tusks and sold them for fifty good Russian rubles. Naturalist Adams heard of the find in 1806.
59632-harper-s-young-people-september-26:
Harper Young People for Tuesday, September 26, 1882, is an illustrated weekly for children, published in New York at four cents. This is volume three, number 152, at a dollar and a half a year in advance. The head opens with a story, Papa Haydn, by Mrs Lillie.

One day nearly a hundred and fifty years ago, the story begins, two elderly gentlemen were dining in an old house in Hamburg. They were music masters of great note, Franck the host, Reuter of Vienna the guest. Their talk was of music. Suddenly Franck declared he had in his house a prodigy, a boy of nine, brought from the country. Reuter was delighted. The boy came in shyly from the kitchen, and stood with hands behind him. Readers get music history told as a childrens story.
8951-scientific-american-volume-17-no-26:
Dated New York, December 28, 1867, this weekly issue of Scientific American reports practical news in art, science, mechanics, chemistry, and manufactures. At three dollars a year, it spoke to inventors, shop men, and curious readers, and it marked the close of its seventeenth volume with notes on patents and the trade.

Contents range from nitro glycerin and hulling hominy to ironclad ships at sea, hand drills, tides, and the great Hoosac Tunnel. Patent claims, shop hints, and an obituary share space with illustrated inventions. The issue is a brisk window on post-Civil War America, busy with making, mending, and patenting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-stoeck:
Albert Stöckl was a neo-Scholastic philosopher and theologian, a thinker in the revived medieval scholastic tradition. He was born at Möhren in Bavaria in March 1823 and died at Eichstätt in November 1895. Educated at Eichstätt, he was ordained a priest in April 1848 and taught philosophy at the episcopal lyceum there. He later taught at Münster in Westphalia, resigned in 1871 amid the divisions of the Vatican Council period, and returned to Eichstätt as cathedral canon and professor.

Stöckl also sat in the lower house of the German Reichstag from 1878 to 1881. His many textbooks covered the whole field of philosophy and circulated widely, including in the United States. Among them were his History of the Philosophy of the Middle Ages in three volumes and his Textbook of Philosophy. His Handbook of the History of Philosophy was translated into English at Dublin in 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurus-von-sc:
Maurus von Schenkl, a Benedictine theologian and canonist born at Auerbach in Bavaria in 1749, died at Amberg in 1816. After the Jesuit college at Amberg he entered Prufening monastery near Ratisbon. He vowed in 1768 and was ordained in 1772. He held monastery offices and served as pastor at Gelgenbach. From 1778 to 1783 he taught dogmatic, moral, and pastoral theology plus canon law at Weltenburg.

In 1783 he became librarian at Prufening, teaching canon law, then moral theology. In 1790 he took a chair in canon law, moral, and pastoral theology at the Amberg lyceum, with the seminary regency. In 1794 he also took the rectorship of the Amberg school, which he gave up in 1798. He declined chairs at Ingolstadt and Aschaffenburg, won the title of spiritual councillor of the king, and after 1808 taught only canon law and pastoral theology. His books on electricity, physics, and chemistry mark a theologian at ease with science.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WRKL_WRKL: Harold Weisberg wrote to the news director of WRKL on July 28, 1966, addressing station staff member George Deere. Part of the letter concerns sales of Weisberg's books on the Kennedy assassination. In 1966 his first attacks on the Warren Report were new, and he promoted them himself. The letter shows a self-published author asking a small station for attention.
scientific-american-volume-17-no-26-dece: Scientific American, a weekly journal of practical information, art, science, mechanics, chemistry, and manufactures, appears here in a late issue of its seventeenth volume. The issue is Number 26, new series, dated New York, December 28, 1867. The price is given as three dollars per annum in advance, and a contents note marks illustrated articles with an asterisk. Listed contents include an improvement in hulling and cleansing hominy, nitro glycerin, Hisert's adjustable cultivator tooth, a remedy for cold feet in city cars, and getting your money back.
